author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Things Steel Cannot Say
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The support beam was making a sound Danse couldn't hear.

Toph told him so three times.

"I know what it feels like," she said, standing barefoot on the workshop floor.

Danse looked at the steel section lying across two supports.

"Then describe the defect."

"It's not broken."

"That's what the measurements show."

"It's tired."

I nearly dropped the notebook.

"Tired?" Danse repeated.

Toph folded her arms.

"You asked me to describe it."

"Metal fatigue is a specific mechanical process."

"Congratulations. You know a fancy name for the thing I'm telling you."

They stared at one another.

I looked at the beam.

The new accessible entrance to Brasswatch Yard had passed its first rain test. Edda could enter without assistance, and the emergency exit opened with one motion. But the overhead support in the adjacent storage room had begun to sag under a load it wasn't designed to carry. Tamsin wanted the replacement verified before anybody moved heavy supplies underneath it.

Danse had brought measurements. Toph had brought her earth sense.

Neither seemed especially interested in the other person's method.

"Can we test the load while the room is empty?" I asked.

Danse nodded.

"Yes, if the supports are braced."

Toph tapped the floor.

"Bracing won't tell you how the beam behaves after three days of rain."

"That's what the corrosion inspection is for."

"Then why are you using dry numbers?"

He opened his mouth.

Closed it.

I waited.

The question wasn't foolish. Toph could sense tiny shifts in the stone beneath the supports, but she couldn't measure the metal's internal stress from its surface alone. Danse could calculate tolerances, but his first measurements had been taken before moisture reached the joints.

Both had part of the answer.

The real problem was that Tamsin's workers had spent two nights keeping the storage room safe while the specialists argued.

I noticed them through the window.

Two people were stacking supplies in a temporary shed, careful to keep the heavier crates on the ground. Their sleeves were damp. One was wearing gloves with a hole in the thumb.

"Who's paying them for the extra shifts?" I asked.

Danse looked up.

"Tamsin arranged the work."

"Did she arrange the pay?"

He hesitated.

Toph turned her head toward the shed.

"That's a good question."

I went outside.

The workers were named Renn and Aster. They had agreed to move supplies for one afternoon. When the repair ran late, they kept helping because the yard needed the space clear. Nobody had told them they were expected to continue without wages, but nobody had checked whether they could afford to keep donating their time.

I asked.

Renn looked embarrassed.

"We can manage one more day," they said.

"That's not what I asked."

Aster rubbed their hands together.

"We need to be paid if this takes much longer."

I nodded.

"Thank you for saying it."

Back inside, I told Danse and Toph.

Danse's face tightened.

"I should have checked."

"Yes," I said.

Toph looked toward the floor.

"Me too."

We stopped the inspection long enough to agree on a labor plan. The storage room would remain closed. The workers would be paid for the additional time already spent, and the next shift would be scheduled only after we knew what needed doing. Neri's public ledger had enough money for safe temporary storage but not a complete replacement. The council would have to approve that expense.

It was uncomfortable.

It was more honest than pretending that a brilliant structural solution could pay a worker's rent.

When the repair testing resumed, Toph and Danse tried again.

Toph placed her hands on the stone support and described the slight movement she felt when a measured load was applied. Danse recorded the deflection and compared it with his calculations. The first result matched.

The second did not.

"There," Toph said.

Danse leaned closer.

"That is outside tolerance."

"That's what I've been saying."

He looked at the number.

"Under the dry test, this beam passed."

"And now?"

"Now it doesn't."

They stared at the data.

Then Danse looked at Toph.

"You were right to insist on another test."

Toph grinned.

"Say it louder. I want the whole yard to hear."

"Don't push your luck."

I smiled.

Tamsin ordered a replacement beam. Danse wrote up the evidence, including the limits of his earlier inspection. Toph added a note about the movement in the stone and asked that the supports be checked again after the next storm.

The storage room remained closed.

We moved the last crates into the temporary shed, this time with a schedule and payment agreed in advance. Aster returned the borrowed gloves and took the wages without having to apologize for needing them.

By evening, Danse was quiet.

I found him cleaning the measuring tools at the workbench. The light from the furnace cast warm shadows across his face.

"Thinking?" I asked.

"Yes."

"About Toph?"

"About how quickly I treated her observations as an insult to my training."

I leaned against the table.

"She did call your numbers dry."

"She was correct."

"That must hurt."

He smiled faintly.

"I used to believe expertise was a rank. Someone either had authority or did not. In the Brotherhood, we trusted chains of command because they made decisions fast."

"And now?"

"Now I think speed can hide the person who pays for it."

He looked toward the shed.

"Renn and Aster shouldn't have had to ask whether their time mattered."

"No."

He took a breath.

"I would like to speak to them tomorrow. Not to make a speech. To ask how the schedule could be better."

I nodded.

"That sounds useful."

He set down the last tool.

"Can I ask something else?"

"Of course."

"Do you still want dinner with me after spending all day watching me be wrong?"

I laughed softly.

"I love you because you're willing to change your mind. Not because you're never wrong."

He looked at me, something warmer moving through his expression.

"Then perhaps I should be wrong more often."

"Please don't. It costs the yard money."

He laughed.

I reached for his hand. His fingers curled around mine, steady and a little rough from work.

We went home along the lit path. The storage room behind us was still unsafe, the beam still needed replacing, and the workers still deserved their wages.

For once, Danse seemed able to let those facts exist without turning them into a personal verdict.

We reached the workshop gate and found the new closure notice posted beneath the lantern. Someone had added a small line to the bottom: workers could report unsafe schedules to the civilian committee, not only to Danse.

He read it twice.

"That wasn't my wording," he said.

"Is that a problem?"

"No. Renn wrote it more clearly."

Renn happened to be leaving with an empty lunch tin. Danse asked whether they had time to discuss the next shift.

"Better than yesterday," Renn said, "but Aster can't work mornings. They have family obligations and nobody asked."

"Then that shift stays open until somebody accepts it," Danse replied.

Renn raised their eyebrows. "You mean it?"

"Yes."

They went to tell Aster. Danse looked after them.

"I kept calling them a unit. As though that meant I knew their lives."

"It doesn't," I said.

"I am learning."

We'd talked about that difference in our own relationship, too. I was ethically non-monogamous, preferred polyamory, and had been explicit that care didn't turn into a chain of command. A plan only worked if the people involved could honestly accept, revise or decline it.

Danse moved a delivery cart away from the accessible path without waiting to be asked. Edda would be pleased, although I suspected he'd rather fight another Brotherhood patrol than accept a public compliment.

"You're smiling," he said.

"Am I?"

"Yes."

"I like the man who asks the worker before assigning the job."

He looked away, but not quickly enough to hide his smile.


The next morning he had already written the updated shift schedule.

Toph arrived, tapped it with one finger, and declared it "almost competent."

He took the compliment.
